before.approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, end of FR 6211 off Chiwawa River Road), start on Phelps Creek Trail #1511. At about a quarter mile the Carne Mountain Trail splits off steeply to the right (skip it); stay on Phelps Creek Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the creek. At 2.6 mi you cross into Glacier Peak Wilderness. Continue to roughly 3.4–3.5 mi, where the trail crosses Leroy Creek (about 4,140 ft) on a log/rock crossing that can run high with snowmelt in early summer — this is the key junction. Immediately after the crossing, leave the maintained trail and turn right (northeast) onto the unmaintained Leroy Creek climbers' trail, which follows the north side of Leroy Creek and gains roughly 2,000 ft in about 1.5 miles of steep, sometimes brushy, boot-track tread — this is the stiffest sustained pitch of the day. It tops out in the open meadows/talus of Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft, a common camp spot with reliable water from Leroy Creek and views of Seven Fingered Jack, Mount Maude, and Ice Lakes basin above. From camp, aim for the broad southwest slope of the peak: two parallel lines lead out of the basin — a rock gully straight up to the lower southwest slope, or a gentler ridge to its right — and they merge in a flat shoulder around 7,200–7,800 ft where the wide, rocky southwest slope proper begins (some parties climb to the base of cliffs near 7,200 ft then cut right to the 7,800 ft bench, which is described as the easiest line). From there it's an extended ascent of loose talus and scree — boulder-hop and pick the cleanest line, favoring rock over scree where possible — trending slightly left up the slope toward the summit rocks, with a few short steeper steps that can be passed on either side without real difficulty. Near the top, cross a shallow ravine below the summit spires and follow a faint climbers' trail up to the left-most (true) summit block at 9,078 ft. Hazards are loose talus/scree underfoot the entire upper mountain, exposed ridge/slope travel above treeline with no shelter from weather, and route-finding that gets harder in poor visibility since there is no single defined trail above Leroy Basin; a lingering snow gully in the entry couloir in early season may require an ice axe. Basin-to-summit is commonly quoted at about 3 hours in good conditions; round trip is roughly 13 miles with 5,600 ft of gain.

before.descent_text: Descend the ascent line in reverse: down the southwest scree/talus slope to the 7,200–7,800 ft bench, then drop back into Leroy Basin via whichever of the rock-gully or ridge lines you prefer (the ridge line is generally more stable underfoot than the loose gully). This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on the standard Southwest Slopes route, so rappels = 0. From Leroy Basin, retrace the steep climbers' trail down along Leroy Creek back to the Phelps Creek Trail junction (roughly 2,000 ft of descent in 1.5 miles on loose, sometimes braided boot-tread — easy to lose the tread on the way down, especially in the lower brushy section), then follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 back out to the trailhead. Watch for: loose, ball-bearing scree on the upper mountain that makes for slow, careful downclimbing and real rockfall risk onto parties below (stay bunched or well-spaced, avoid stacking climbers directly below each other in the gully); lingering steep snow in the entry couloir/gully in early-to-mid season, which some parties glissade but which has rock runout hazard lower down; and the general difficulty of route-finding the correct braid of the Leroy Creek climbers' trail in the timber below the basin, particularly at dusk or in poor visibility. No technical rope work is required for this route in typical summer conditions.
